svg.aria-label: Diagram: Cloud DNS public zones in Google Cloud and what it actually takes to be authoritative for a domain; a public zone is visible to the internet and Cloud DNS answers queries for it from public authoritative name servers, which is why public zones cannot forward and must be authoritative; Cloud DNS creates the NS and SOA records at the zone apex automatically and they cannot be deleted through the API, which is also why a CNAME can never sit at the apex since a CNAME must exist on its own; creating the zone does nothing until you change the name servers at your domain registrar, where you should supply all of them rather than the minimum of two, and resolvers keep using the old name servers until the TTL on the old NS records expires; every public managed zone is assigned to one of five name server shards, so you can create at most five zones with the same DNS name and at most five levels of subdomains, a limit that applies across all projects and users in Google Cloud, which is why parent zones must be created before their subdomains and why the last free shard requires TXT domain-ownership verification; and DNSSEC must be enabled in three places, the zone, the TLD registry through a DS record at your registrar, and a validating resolver, so turning DNSSEC on in Cloud DNS alone has no effect
svg.title: Cloud DNS public zones: creating the zone is the easy half; the authority is granted elsewhere
svg.text: Creating the zone takes one command. Becoming authoritative happens at your registrar.
And two of the limits that shape it are not in your project at all.
What a public zone is
“A public zone is visible to the internet.” Cloud DNS answers for it from PUBLIC AUTHORITATIVE
name servers, “regardless of where the queries originate.”
Which is why there is no forwarding here: “Cloud DNS does not support DNS forwarding for public
zones. Cloud DNS public zones must be authoritative.” Authority is the whole product.
The apex is occupied before you add a single record
“Cloud DNS automatically creates NS and SOA records at the zone apex.” You cannot delete them,
and you must not change the NS record or the name servers Cloud DNS selected.
CONSEQUENCE: a CNAME can never sit at the apex. A CNAME “must always exist on its own” — and
NS and SOA are already there. This is RFC 1034, not a Google restriction.
Console detail: @ does NOT create an apex record. Leave the DNS name field BLANK.
The zone does nothing until the registrar points at it
“Different managed zones have different name servers.” Read yours; do not assume a pattern.
“Typically, you must provide AT LEAST TWO” — but “to benefit from Cloud DNS’s high availability,
you must use ALL the name servers.” The minimum and the correct answer are different numbers.
Cutover is not instant: resolvers keep using the OLD name servers until the old NS TTL expires.
Name server shards — the limit that is not in your project
“Cloud DNS assigns every public managed zone to one of FIVE name server shards.” The shard is the
letter: ns-cloud-e1 through ns-cloud-e4 are the E shard. Five shards x four servers = 20 in total.
A zone cannot land on a shard already holding the same name, a subdomain of it, or its parent.
So: at most FIVE zones with the same DNS name, and FIVE levels of subdomains.
“These limitations apply to ALL PROJECTS AND USERS in Google Cloud.” Strangers’ zones can consume
your shards. The last free one needs TXT domain-ownership verification before it is granted.
THE RULE: create the PARENT zone before any subdomain zone — even if the parent is hosted
elsewhere. Subdomains in all five shards means the parent can never be created.
Recovery exists, and it is an export, a re-delegation, a TTL wait and a restore. Avoid it.
DNSSEC is three switches, and you own only the first
1. THE ZONE — Cloud DNS “automatically manages the creation and rotation of DNSSEC keys” and the
signing of zone data with RRSIG records. One toggle, nothing to operate.
2. THE TLD REGISTRY — a DS record authenticating your DNSKEY, added through your registrar.
3. THE RESOLVER — full protection needs a resolver that validates signatures.
“If you cannot add a DS record through your domain registrar … enabling DNSSEC has NO EFFECT.”
The shape to carry out of this post: on a public zone, three of the things that decide whether it
works are outside Google Cloud — the registrar’s name server list, the TLD registry’s DS record,
and the resolver’s willingness to validate. The console shows all three as green on its side.
A fourth, the shard, is inside Google Cloud but not inside your project.
